lead: 19 days of gunpowder, ephemeral art, flowers and fire. Valencia’s biggest festival combines critical satire, centuries-old tradition and the most impressive pyrotechnic show in Europe.

The Fallas are, above all, a neighbourhood festival that scales up into a global spectacle. Each falla commission — an association of long-time neighbours — works all year round to put up its monument in the street, organise events at its clubhouse and represent its neighbourhood at the festival. This popular, citizen-based structure is what makes the Fallas genuinely different from any other celebration in the world.

For the visitor, the Fallas are a superposition of experiences: the ground vibrating with the mascletà, the smell of gunpowder mixed with that of buñuelos, the night-time stroll among illuminated fallas, the thrill of watching burn in minutes what took months to build. There is no festival in the world that combines art, pyrotechnics, tradition and community in this way.

items.title: La Crida
items.subtitle: The official proclamation · Start of the Fallas · Serranos Towers
items.body: The festival officially kicks off on the last Sunday of February with the Crida — “call” in Valencian —, the event in which the Falleras Mayores of Valencia, from the top of the Serranos Towers, encourage the whole city and the world to join the Fallas. It is the official starting gun that opens weeks of gunpowder, art and celebration in the street. The Crida is one of the most moving events for the falleros and falleras, who listen from the streets of the historic centre to the message of their highest representatives.
facts: Serranos Towers · Last Sunday of February · Free access

items.title: The Mascletà
items.subtitle: 19 mascletàs · 120 decibels · The daily ritual of fire
items.body: The mascletà is the ritual that marks the pulse of each day during the 19 days of the Fallas. At 14:00 sharp, the Fallera Mayor steps out onto the City Hall balcony and speaks the magic words: “Senyor pirotècnic, pot començar la mascletà”. And then the ground and the air vibrate at the same time for ten minutes with hundreds of kilos of gunpowder reaching 120 decibels. It is not a visual spectacle: it is a physical, sensory experience that you feel in your chest. A different pyrotechnic firm signs its mascletà each day, and the rivalry between them is part of the legend. Essential trick: keep your mouth slightly open to cushion the pressure.
facts: Plaza del Ayuntamiento · 14:00 from 1 to 19 March · Free access · Arrive 30 min early

items.title: L’Albà and the Plantà
items.subtitle: The magical set-up · More than 400 monuments in a single night
items.body: The night of 15 to 16 March is one of the most magical of the Fallas. At 23:59 on the 15th, the Nit de l’Albà opens the Fallas Week with all the city’s pyrotechnic firms firing simultaneously — a tradition revived in 2016. From that moment, the 397 falla commissions work non-stop so that by dawn on the 16th all the monuments are in place. The fallas can reach between 14 and 20 metres in height — the equivalent of a five-storey building. At dawn, the jury tours the city and rewards the best. Seeing the city transformed in the small hours, with the falleros still assembling their works, is a unique experience.
facts: Night of 15 to 16 · From 9:00 on the 16th all the monuments can already be visited

items.title: The Ninot Indultat · Ninot Exhibition
items.subtitle: The only figure saved from the fire · Popular vote · Fallero Museum
items.body: Each falla commission contributes a figure — the ninot — to the Ninot Exhibition, held in the Sala Arquerías of the Museu de les Ciències (CAC). The public votes on which deserves to be saved from the cremà. The winner, the ninot indultat, is the only figure in the whole festival that will not burn: it goes straight to the Fallero Museum, where all the indultats since 1934 are kept. The popular verdict for the children’s ninot is read out on 14 March and the adults’ on 15 March. The exhibition charges admission (€3) and is one of the most accessible ways to see the artistic level of the falla monuments before they burn.
facts: Exhibition: CAC Museu de les Ciències · €3 · Verdict: 14–15 March · Fallero Museum: free, closed Mondays

items.title: L’Ofrenda de Flores
items.subtitle: Plaza de la Virgen · 15-metre tapestry · The most moving event of the Fallas
items.body: For two consecutive days, 17 and 18 March, thousands of falleros and falleras walk through the city dressed in traditional Valencian costume, from their neighbourhoods to the Plaza de la Virgen, to lay flowers at the feet of the Virgen de los Desamparados. The flowers, arranged by the commissions according to that year’s design, gradually form a mantle which by the end reaches 15 metres in height above the image. The scent of the flowers, the music of the bands, the colour of the costumes and the emotion of the falleros make the Ofrenda the most heartfelt and universally recognised event of the Fallas. The tapestry can be visited until 20 March.
facts: Plaza de la Virgen · 17 and 18 March · Free access · 15 m tapestry visitable until the 20th

items.title: La Nit del Foc · Fireworks Displays
items.subtitle: Firework displays · Nit del Foc on the 18th · 20+ minutes of spectacle
items.body: The nights of Fallas Week are lit up by firework displays fired from the Monteolivete bridge, next to the City of Arts and Sciences. At 23:59 on the central days, the Valencia sky becomes a canvas of light and colour. The most eagerly awaited is the Nit del Foc — the night of fire — on 18 March: more than 20 minutes of fireworks that draw hundreds of thousands of spectators along the Turia Garden. It is the biggest pyrotechnic show of the whole festival and one of the most impressive in Spain.
facts: Turia Garden (Alameda) · 16–18 March · 00:00 · Nit del Foc: 18 March · Free access

items.title: La Cremà
items.subtitle: The grand finale · Everything burns · Children’s fallas 20:00 · Main fallas 22:00
items.body: On the night of 19 March, Saint Joseph’s Day, the cremà arrives: the moment when each falla burns in front of the firefighters and the very falleros who built it over months. It is the most thrilling and paradoxical event of the festival: ephemeral art consumed in minutes before the eyes of those who worked on it hardest. At 20:00 the children’s fallas start to burn; at 22:00 the main ones; at 22:30 the Special Section first prize; and at 23:00 the falla of the Plaza del Ayuntamiento, the last to burn, with firefighters wetting the façade of City Hall. The ideal strategy: do the cremà route hopping from neighbourhood to neighbourhood.
facts: Children’s: 20:00 · Main: 22:00 · SE 1st prize: 22:30 · City Hall: 23:00

blocks.title: Tips for experiencing the Fallas like a Valencian
items: For the mascletà, arrive at the Plaza del Ayuntamiento 30 min early and keep your mouth slightly open to cushion the 120 decibels
The Nit de l’Albà on 15 March and the Nit del Foc on the 18th are the most impressive firework displays — choose your spot in the Turia Garden in advance
The cremà route on 19 March: hop from neighbourhood to neighbourhood — the smaller fallas burn earlier and have a more intimate, moving atmosphere
Visit the fallas at night: the lighting transforms them completely and the atmosphere in the neighbourhoods is incomparable
Pumpkin buñuelos with chocolate are the fallero breakfast and afternoon snack par excellence — look for them at any street stall
Book accommodation months in advance: during Fallas Week (15–19 March) prices multiply and everything sells out
